panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (a, b, c). a: Real patient clinical photograph of the dorsum of both hands showing tense, monomorphic pustules at a uniform stage of evolution with surrounding hyperpigmentation and edema. The article title identifies this as the first Clade Ib Mpox case in Kinshasa, and the caption describes classic mpox pustular lesions asymmetrically distributed on the extremities. Disease attribution and findings are directly supported. [raw subtype: Clade Ib] b: Real patient clinical photograph of both palms showing high-density asymmetrical pustules with confluence into pseudobullous lesions, a classic palmar mpox manifestation. Attribution to Clade Ib mpox is supported by the disease-specific article title together with the captioned palmar pustular eruption. [raw subtype: Clade Ib] c: Real patient clinical photograph of the dorsum of the foot showing isolated pustules all at the same stage of evolution, consistent with the synchronous monomorphic mpox eruption...

in_text_mentions: Four days later, a vesicle appeared on the pricked finger (Figure 1, panel A), and monkeypox virus (MPXV) was identified in its fluid by PCR, showing a cycle threshold (Ct) of 28. The HCW was sent on sick leave, with indication for the institution of contact and droplet isolation measures at home.

On the sixth day of illness, fever (temperature 38.4°C), chills, and malaise developed and lasted for ≈48 hours. The finger lesion became pustular and painful and showed surrounding erythema and swelling (Figure 1, panel B). A tender, indurated, erythematous and well-delimited linear streak from the left finger to the armpit appeared on the seventh day (Figure 2, panel A), without regional adenopathy. MPXV PCR was repeated in samples from the oropharynx and blood; again, results were negative.

By the 18th day of illness, all skin lesions, except the one on the left index finger, had evolved through the pustular stage into crust. The index lesion became necrotic (Figure 1, panel C) and was debrided on the 24th day of illness, showing a necrotic scab that had a diameter of 0.5 cm underneath the devitalized tissue (Figure 1, panel D). An MPXV PCR result was still positive in the crust and showed a Ct of 23, but viral culture was negative.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Real-patient clinical photograph from a laboratory-confirmed Mpox case; caption explicitly states the images depict Mpox lesions in pustular stage. Umbilicated pustules on the hand dorsum are the textbook cutaneous presentation of mpox. The prior triage's 'other disease' label is superseded by the panel-specific caption evidence attributing the lesions to Mpox, which is a configured target disease. B: Real-patient clinical photograph; caption explicitly attributes the palmar pustules to Mpox and calls firm pearly palmar pustules a recognised feature of Mpox. Palmar involvement is a classic, well-recognized mpox cutaneous manifestation. C: Real-patient clinical photograph from the same laboratory-confirmed Mpox case; caption attributes the scattered trunk and abdominal lesions to Mpox in pustular and crusting stages. panels.figure_caption: Cutaneous lesions Representative clinical photographs of cutaneous lesions obtained on hospital day 9, following laboratory confirmation of Mpox and after dedicated written informed consent for clinical photography and publication had been obtained from the patient. The images depict Mpox lesions in pustular and early crusting stages, consistent with the natural evolution of lesions approximately one week after their initial appearance. Panel A: dorsum of the hand with umbilicated pustular lesions; Panel B: palmar surface with firm pearly pustules, a recognised feature of Mpox; Panel C: trunk and lower abdomen showing scattered lesions in pustular and crusting stages, illustrating the polymorphic appearance characteristic of the current outbreak phenotype. All images were captured on the same day of illness (hospital day 9).
